newsitem.title: USA: Progress looks slow at EU, U.S. meat talks.
newsitem.headline: Progress looks slow at EU, U.S. meat talks.

text.p: U.S. and European negotiators met for more than seven hours on Tuesday to settle an escalating dispute over meat import inspection regulations, but U.S. industry sources said Wednesday it did not appear that much progress had been made in the talks.
Officials met until after 2100 EDT Tuesday night and began meeting again Wednesday at 1300 EDT, an Agriculture Department spokesman said.

The negotiators remain stuck on a handful of key points, said sources close to the talks. An agreement over eggs and dairy shipments appears close at hand, but on the bigger poultry and meat issues, sources did not report any movement.
"Not a whole lot happened ... I'm just not that optimistic," said a U.S. industry official who had been briefed on the Tuesday session.
European officials agreed there were still problems remaining.
"We're still very much at it," said EU spokeswoman Ella Krucoff. "A few things have gone well, but there are still some important outstanding isues to resolve."
Krucoff said that the EU negotiating team is scheduled to return to Brussels Thursday afternoon, but added that if progress is being made, officials would remain in Washington for more talks.
The negotiators have been trying to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks which ended last week without agreement by an April 1 deadline.
The unsuccessful conclusion of last week's talks prompted moves on both sides to restrict bilateral meat and poultry trade.

The European Union on April 1 adopted new poultry import inspection standards that immediately halted U.S. poultry shipments to the EU, and could mean the loss of up to $100 million worth of poultry and dairy sales.

In response to the new EU rules, the United States implemented new regulations that require EU meat and poultry plants to comply with U.S. inspection standards by April 15 or they will not be able to continue exporting to the U.S.
The new U.S. regulations could halt some $300 million worth of imports of European meat products, mostly Danish pork products and Italian hams.
Negotiators are now trying to reach an agreement before April 15 when Washington has said it will remove over 100 EU plants from its list of approved exporters.

One of the key issues left to be resolved is the decontamination process used by U.S. poultry and meat processors -- especially poultry packers -- and the EU's stance against using small amounts of chlorine in rinse water to remove any bacteria.

Also being fought over is the use of wooden pallets in the U.S. packing industry as opposed to plastic pallets used by the Europeans. The EU is calling for the use of plastic pallets in U.S. plants. The U.S. industry contends that the pallets are used to moved boxes of the product, never touch the raw product and have never been proven to spread any disease or bacteria.

Finally, the U.S. meat industry is concerned over the role of EU inspectors in the U.S. plant inspection approval process. The industry says USDA's Food Safety Inspection Service should be recognized as the primary authority to approve U.S. plants, and that EU inspectors should only be involved in reviews and auditing, as U.S. inspectors have functioned in Euopre.
